title: Photorefractive keratectomy (PRK)
subtitle: Epithelial removal, excimer surface ablation and bandage contact lens

indications: Stable myopia, hypermetropia or astigmatism within the laser's treatment range, in an adult who wants less dependence on glasses or contact lenses.
Preferred over LASIK for thin corneas, contact sports or occupations with risk of eye trauma, and anterior basement membrane disease.
contraindications: Keratoconus or suspicious topography, unstable refraction, active ocular surface or autoimmune disease affecting healing.
Pregnancy and breastfeeding; unrealistic expectations; severe dry eye.
preparation: Stable refraction, cycloplegic refraction, topography and tomography, pachymetry, pupil size, dry eye assessment.
Contact lenses out for the agreed period before measurements.
Consent: pain for two to four days, slower visual recovery than LASIK, haze, regression, glare and halos, dry eye, infection, and that reading glasses will still be needed with age.
positioning: Supine under the laser, head level with the chin and forehead in one plane; the fellow eye covered.
equipment: Excimer laser with eye tracker, lid speculum, 20% alcohol and well or an epithelial brush (or a transepithelial laser profile), Weck sponges, mitomycin C 0.02% per protocol, chilled balanced salt, bandage contact lens.
anatomy: The corneal epithelium, Bowman's layer and the anterior stroma; the pupil centre and the visual axis.
Surface ablation leaves the whole residual stroma untouched by a flap, so the cornea stays stronger than after LASIK.
criticalSafety: Treat the right eye with the right programme: confirm patient, eye and refraction at the laser.
Centre on the pupil or visual axis with the tracker engaged.
Keep mitomycin C to the agreed time and wash it off.
commonErrors: An uneven epithelial removal giving an irregular ablation.
complications: Infective keratitis under the bandage lens.
Over- or under-correction, glare and halos, dry eye.
postop: Bandage lens until the epithelium has healed (usually four to five days); antibiotic and steroid drops on a taper; analgesia.
Same-day return for increasing pain, discharge or falling vision (infective keratitis).
Protect from ultraviolet light; review refraction over three months.

steps.emphasis: Elective surgery on healthy eyes: written consent at a separate visit, with a cooling-off period per standards.
At the laser: patient name, eye, refraction and treatment profile read aloud from the plan.
Supine under the laser, head level, chin and forehead in one plane; fellow eye covered.
Clean the lids and tape or drape the lashes away from the field.
Bandage lens in, drops explained, and the warning that increasing pain or discharge after day two is infection until proven otherwise.

step.prk.epithelium.title: Removing the epithelium
step.prk.epithelium.why: The laser must treat bare, evenly exposed stroma. An irregular epithelial removal or one that lets alcohol reach the limbus gives an irregular result and slow healing.
how: Remove the epithelium over the planned zone: 20% alcohol in a well for about 20 to 30 seconds then a sponge sweep, a rotating brush, or a transepithelial laser profile.
Dry the alcohol up and irrigate so none spills onto the limbus.
Work quickly so the stroma does not dry out before the ablation.

step.prk.mmc.title: Mitomycin C to reduce haze (when indicated)
step.prk.mmc.why: After deeper ablations, haze can blur vision for months. A brief application of dilute mitomycin C reduces it, but too long harms the corneal cells.
how: Apply a sponge soaked in mitomycin C 0.02% to the ablated area for the time in the protocol (often 12 to 30 seconds).
Irrigate thoroughly with chilled balanced salt.

step.prk.bandage.title: Bandage contact lens
step.prk.bandage.why: The bandage lens reduces pain and protects the new epithelium. It is also a place for bacteria to grow, so it needs drops and a removal date.
how: Place a soft bandage contact lens and check it centres and moves slightly.
Start antibiotic and steroid drops; give the removal date in writing.
pitfalls: A tight lens that does not move.
